paragraphs: Training a neural network across several machines creates two connected challenges: unstable gradients can slow optimization, while frequent communication can reduce the benefit of parallel work. This paper studies whether gradient clipping, which limits unusually large updates, can address the first problem while allowing machines to communicate less often.

The proposed algorithm performs multiple clipped gradient updates on each machine before exchanging information. Its analysis uses a relaxed smoothness assumption on the loss landscape, rather than requiring the usual globally controlled gradient variation. This accommodates the combination of nonconvex optimization, large gradients, and skipped communication rounds that makes the distributed setting difficult.

For homogeneous data across machines, the authors prove an iteration complexity of O(1/(N epsilon^4)) and communication complexity of O(1/epsilon^3) for reaching an epsilon-stationary point. The dependence on the number of machines N establishes linear parallel speedup under those conditions. Experiments across several benchmark datasets and scenarios also show fast convergence, supporting the practical relevance of the theoretical result.
neurips-2022-a-communication-efficient-d.tldr: Distributed gradient clipping achieves provable parallel speedup with fewer communication rounds under relaxed smoothness and homogeneous data assumptions.

paragraphs: Unsupervised reinforcement learning prepares an agent for later tasks without giving it a task reward during preparation. Many methods supply an internal reward based on surprise instead. Seeking surprising experiences encourages exploration, whereas reducing surprise encourages the agent to gain control over its environment.

The paper argues that choosing either direction alone depends on assumptions about how unpredictable the environment's dynamics are. Those assumptions can be difficult to justify when an agent encounters an unfamiliar environment. MOSS addresses the dilemma with a mixture of policies: one component learns to maximize surprise, and another learns to minimize it. The opposing objectives are therefore assigned to different components of the mixture.

This construction avoids committing to an assumption that the environment's dynamics have either high or low entropy. On the URLB benchmark, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and improvements over earlier methods based purely on maximizing surprise. The findings support combining exploration and control objectives when preparing policies for adaptation, rather than selecting a single surprise objective in advance.
neurips-2022-a-mixture-of-surprises-for-.tldr: MOSS combines surprise-seeking and surprise-reducing policies to prepare agents for downstream tasks without assuming a particular level of environmental unpredictability.

paragraphs: Recovering a person's three-dimensional pose and body shape depends on more than the choice of prediction algorithm. This study examines how datasets, backbone networks, and training choices affect human mesh recovery. Its motivation is that weak configurations can make comparisons between new algorithms less fair and less informative.

Across 31 datasets, the authors find that particular data attributes matter: varied poses, body shapes, camera characteristics, and backbone features contribute differently to performance. Selecting and combining suitable datasets can substantially improve results. Experiments with ten backbones, spanning convolutional networks and transformers, also show that knowledge learned on a closely related task transfers readily to human mesh recovery.

The study further identifies augmentation and loss design as important training decisions. Combining its findings, the authors obtain a PA-MPJPE of 47.3 millimeters on the 3DPW test set with a relatively simple model. The contribution is both a stronger set of comparison baselines and practical guidance for configuring training, showing why algorithm evaluations should account for the surrounding experimental setup.
neurips-2022-benchmarking-and-analyzing-.tldr: A broad benchmark shows that data selection, backbone transfer, and training design can substantially strengthen human mesh recovery without a complex new algorithm.

paragraphs: Chromatic correlation clustering organizes objects whose pairwise relationships belong to different categories. The input is a graph in which objects are nodes and relationship categories are represented by edge colors. This extends ordinary correlation clustering to settings where the relationships carry more categorical information, with applications in data mining, social networks, and bioinformatics.

The paper improves the theoretical guarantee available for this problem using a linear programming approach. It establishes a 2.5-approximation, improving the previously best known factor of 3. The smaller approximation factor gives a tighter worst-case guarantee relative to an optimal solution; it is a statement about solution quality, rather than a claim that the algorithm always finds the optimum.

The authors also develop an efficient heuristic based on greedy clustering and evaluate its effectiveness and efficiency in extensive experiments. This supplies a practical algorithm alongside the theoretical advance. These are distinct contributions: the approximation result strengthens the formal understanding of the problem, while the heuristic experiments address how well the proposed practical strategy works.
neurips-2022-chromatic-correlation-clust.tldr: The paper improves chromatic correlation clustering's approximation guarantee from 3 to 2.5 and introduces an experimentally effective greedy heuristic.

paragraphs: Long tasks require an agent to connect many individual actions to more distant objectives. Hierarchical reinforcement learning tries to make this manageable by introducing intermediate goals, but those goals often require human design. Director learns hierarchical behavior from visual input by planning within the internal representation of a learned world model.

Its high-level policy chooses goals in that representation while pursuing both task and exploration rewards. A low-level policy learns to reach the selected goals. This division allows goal selection and goal execution to be learned together without manually specifying a goal space. Although goals are represented internally, the world model can decode them into images, making the high-level decisions available for visual inspection.

Director learns successful behavior across visual control environments, Atari games, and DMLab levels. It also outperforms exploration methods on very sparse-reward tasks. These include a quadruped navigating a three-dimensional maze using an egocentric camera and proprioception, without the global position or overhead view used in prior work. The results demonstrate useful learned hierarchy across several demanding settings.
neurips-2022-deep-hierarchical-planning-.tldr: Director learns visual hierarchies by choosing goals inside a world model and training a lower-level policy to achieve them.

paragraphs: When comparing two conditions, useful differences may involve groups of related features rather than isolated measurements. DiSC is designed to find such groups. Its central idea is to examine how relationships among features change between conditions, using those changes to identify subsets that distinguish the conditions.

The method builds a separate graph for each condition. Each node represents a feature, and connections are weighted according to feature similarity within that condition. A spectral procedure then searches for groups of nodes whose connection patterns differ substantially between the two graphs. This makes the organization of features part of the selection process, rather than considering only individual features independently.

The authors analyze the approach through a simplified example based on the stochastic block model. They also test it on MNIST, hyperspectral images, simulated single-cell RNA sequencing data, and task-based functional MRI. Across these evaluations, DiSC identifies features that distinguish conditions better than competing methods. The results support comparing condition-specific feature relationships as a useful route to discovering informative groups.
neurips-2022-disc-differential-spectral-.tldr: DiSC finds groups of discriminative features by comparing their similarity graphs across two conditions.

paragraphs: A recommender can influence both what someone consumes now and what they prefer later. This paper models recommendations as menus offered to an agent whose choices depend on previous consumption. The system must earn reward while ensuring that the distribution of items actually selected remains sufficiently diverse, measured through entropy.

The formulation is an adversarial bandit problem: the recommender observes the chosen item and its reward, but does not know the agent's preference model. The analysis focuses on locally learnable preferences, meaning behavior across the domain can be estimated from observations in a small region. Bounded-degree polynomial models and functions with sparse Fourier representations fall within this class.

For that class, the algorithm achieves approximately T^(3/4) regret, up to logarithmic factors, against sufficiently diverse item distributions realizable through menus at every history. The authors connect these requirements by showing that sufficiently high-entropy distributions are realizable in this sense. Runtime and regret lower bounds explain why the learning assumptions and comparison benchmark matter to the guarantee.
neurips-2022-diversified-recommendations.tldr: The paper gives a conditional regret guarantee for recommendations that balance reward and consumption diversity as user preferences adapt.

paragraphs: Many selection problems involve diminishing returns: adding an item helps less once similar benefits are already covered. Monotone submodular maximization formalizes this structure. This paper considers the harder situation where the value of a chosen set can only be evaluated through a noisy oracle, so the algorithm cannot rely on exact comparisons.

The authors develop a local search framework that accounts for noise and construct smoothed substitute objectives to reduce its effect. For a cardinality constraint, which limits the number of selected items, their algorithm achieves an approximation of 1-1/e-O(epsilon) for any positive epsilon. It requires only polynomially many queries to the noisy oracle, improving an earlier exponential query requirement.

The analysis also covers general matroid constraints, a broader framework for specifying which selections are permitted. Here the authors establish the first constant-factor approximation in the stated noisy setting. Together, the results show that carefully designed local search and smoothing can preserve meaningful optimization guarantees even when objective evaluations are distorted.
neurips-2022-efficient-submodular-optimi.tldr: Noise-aware local search and smoothing give efficient approximation guarantees for constrained submodular maximization with noisy evaluations.

paragraphs: A network's initialization can influence how its parameters move throughout training. This paper investigates that dependence for three-layer ReLU networks as their width grows toward infinity. The authors derive a normalized gradient flow and identify two independent quantities that distinguish training behavior for common initialization methods.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets identify three regimes for individual layers. In the linear regime, the relative change in a neuron's incoming weights and bias tends toward zero as width increases. In the condensed regime, that relative change diverges. A critical regime separates them, with changes remaining of constant order. These categories describe parameter dynamics, rather than simply classifying final prediction quality.

A key observation is that different layers in the same network can occupy different regimes during training. In condensed regimes, weights also concentrate along isolated orientations with low complexity. The empirical phase diagram therefore suggests that deeper networks can combine qualitatively different layer behaviors. It offers guidance for studying initialization while preserving the distinction between observed three-layer results and broader possibilities for deep networks.
neurips-2022-empirical-phase-diagram-for.tldr: Experiments map three initialization-dependent training regimes and show that separate layers can exhibit different dynamics within one network.

paragraphs: Strong game performance does not by itself explain what a learning system represents internally. This paper examines AlphaZero in Hex to investigate whether and where its network captures strategically meaningful concepts. AlphaZero combines a neural network with Monte Carlo tree search, so the authors also examine how conceptual knowledge emerges across these two components.

They adapt model probing and behavioral tests from natural language processing. These tools add ways to evaluate learned representations and behavior beyond the final measure of playing strength. The aim is to build a fuller account of the system's strengths and weaknesses, including how concepts appear during learning and where they are represented within the network.

In the Hex analyses, tree search discovers concepts before the neural network learns to encode them. Concepts involving short-term end-game planning are best represented in the final layers, while longer-term planning concepts appear in middle layers. These findings reveal structure within this system and motivate testable hypotheses about learning more generally, rather than establishing a universal pattern for all reinforcement learning models.
neurips-2022-evaluation-beyond-task-perf.tldr: Probes and behavioral tests reveal when and where AlphaZero learns Hex concepts beyond what its playing strength alone shows.

paragraphs: A recommender may need to estimate purchase probability long before it knows whether a purchase occurred. Waiting for complete conversion labels makes training less timely. This paper investigates how user behavior after a click can provide useful earlier evidence, alongside the early conversions that previous methods emphasize.

The generalized delayed feedback model treats both sources as stochastic post-click information within one framework. This allows efficient streaming training as information arrives. The authors also analyze the performance loss from delayed feedback as two components: a temporal gap and a sampling gap. That perspective connects the timing of a signal with how much data is needed to learn effectively from it.

Based on the analysis, the method assesses post-click information using temporal distance together with sample complexity. It then reweights the training objective to emphasize signals that are both informative and timely. Experiments on public datasets support the analysis and demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to organize and prioritize partial evidence while final conversion outcomes are still delayed.
neurips-2022-generalized-delayed-feedbac.tldr: GDFM improves timely conversion prediction by combining early conversions and other post-click signals and weighting their usefulness.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes difficult when an objective has both irregular local geometry and multiple competing regions of improvement. For nonsmooth, nonconvex problems, even defining a useful computational stopping target can be challenging. This paper develops methods that do not require gradients and gives finite-time guarantees for an appropriate notion of approximate stationarity.

The theoretical starting point connects the Goldstein subdifferential with uniform smoothing. This relationship provides a basis for designing gradient-free algorithms around a smoothed objective while targeting Goldstein stationary points of the original problem. The authors introduce both deterministic and stochastic methods for a class of Lipschitz objectives.

Both methods have an expected convergence rate of O(d^(3/2) delta^(-1) epsilon^(-4)) for returning a (delta, epsilon)-Goldstein stationary point, where d is dimension. This is a stationarity guarantee, not a guarantee of finding a global optimum. Two-phase variants improve large-deviation results, strengthening the treatment of outcomes beyond the expectation. Experiments with a two-phase stochastic variant on ReLU-network training demonstrate its effectiveness in that application.
neurips-2022-gradient-free-methods-for-d.tldr: The paper links smoothing to Goldstein stationarity and derives finite-time guarantees for gradient-free nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes harder when an expert and a learner operate in different domains, such as different environments or different kinds of agents. Directly matching their observed states can mix task information with irrelevant domain differences. This paper develops a framework for transferring demonstrated behavior without additional demonstrations or further domain knowledge.

The framework jointly trains the learner's policy and a mapping between the expert and learner domains through adversarial training. A mutual information criterion guides the construction of an expert-state embedding that retains task-relevant information while being invariant to domain-specific details. The embedding therefore gives the mapping problem a more focused representation to work with.

According to the authors, this representation substantially simplifies estimating the cross-domain mapping and supports end-to-end learning. Their experiments demonstrate policy transfer between considerably different domains, including settings where other methods fail, without extra supervision such as additional demonstrations. The central result is that learning what information matters for the task can make imitation feasible even when expert and learner observations differ substantially.
neurips-2022-learn-what-matters-cross-do.tldr: Task-relevant embeddings help agents imitate experts across substantially different domains without extra demonstrations or domain knowledge.

paragraphs: Neural processes are models for learning across tasks that can make predictions at test time without gradient updates. They formulate exchangeable stochastic processes, making them useful for meta learning. This paper identifies a restriction in many existing variants: placing too much representational emphasis on a single global latent variable.

The authors argue that this emphasis weakens approximation power, particularly when the underlying data-generating processes are complicated. Their proposed Mixture of Expert Neural Processes combines neural processes with mixture-of-experts models to construct more expressive exchangeable processes. The change targets the capacity of the learned representation, allowing the model to represent task structure through a mixture of experts.

The resulting models are evaluated on both few-shot supervised learning and meta reinforcement learning. The reported experiments show strong generalization to previously unseen tasks within those benchmarks. This matters because both settings require knowledge acquired across tasks to support a new task with limited task-specific experience. The findings support the proposed mixture as a way to broaden neural-process representations for these applications.
neurips-2022-learning-expressive-meta-re.tldr: Mixture of Expert Neural Processes expands neural-process representations and shows strong generalization on few-shot and meta reinforcement learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Physical prediction benefits from respecting symmetry, but the appropriate symmetry depends on the environment. Gravity, for example, introduces a preferred direction. This paper argues that existing graph-based simulators can encode too little symmetry or impose excessive equivariance when an external field has already broken part of it.

The proposed Subequivariant Graph Neural Network accommodates such fields while retaining a theoretical universal approximation property. It represents objects through particles and introduces object-aware message passing to capture interactions among objects of different shapes, sizes, and properties. A hierarchical organization also supports long-range and complex interactions. These design choices address both physical symmetry and the structure of interacting objects.

On Physion, the model improves contact prediction accuracy by an average of over 3% across eight scenarios compared with state-of-the-art graph simulators. On RigidFall, it reports twofold lower rollout mean squared error. The authors also report strong generalization and data efficiency. The results support matching architectural symmetry to the physical setting while explicitly accounting for object structure.
neurips-2022-learning-physical-dynamics-.tldr: A subequivariant graph network accounts for gravity and object structure to improve learned physical simulation.

paragraphs: Developing abusive-content detectors for Indic languages has been constrained by datasets with limited size and language coverage. This paper contributes both a larger annotated resource and a pretrained detection model. The aim is to support research on identifying harmful comments across languages used by a substantial population of social media users.

The MACD dataset contains 150,000 human-annotated comments from ShareChat, covering five languages and 70,000 users. Abusive content accounts for 49% of the dataset. In addition to annotations, the release includes mappings among comment, post, and user identifiers. Those links make it possible to study relationships among comments, their surrounding posts, and users rather than relying only on isolated comment text.

The authors also release AbuseXLMR, pretrained on social media comments in more than fifteen Indic languages. It outperforms XLM-R and MuRIL on multiple Indic datasets. Monolingual, cross-lingual, and few-shot baselines accompany the release, giving researchers comparison points for studying learning within a language, transfer across languages, and settings with limited labeled examples.
neurips-2022-multilingual-abusive-commen.tldr: MACD and AbuseXLMR provide multilingual data, pretrained modeling, and comparison baselines for abusive-comment detection in Indic languages.

paragraphs: Diffusion models learn to reverse a process that progressively adds noise to data. Their reverse process ultimately produces a sample, but the role played by small amounts of noise during that process is less clear. This paper studies that behavior to better understand how image generation and denoising relate.

The authors observe a fluid transition in the reverse process. One part behaves as though it is generating a still-corrupted image from noise; another behaves as though it is cleaning that image into the final sample. Describing the transition as fluid matters: the observation motivates a functional distinction without asserting a rigid, universal boundary between the two roles.

Based on this finding, the authors propose separating a diffusion model into a generator and a denoiser. The generator remains diffusion-based with its own parameters, while a denoising autoencoder could implement the cleanup component. Experiments validate the proposal and examine both advantages and disadvantages. The contribution is an experimentally investigated decomposition of diffusion behavior, rather than a claim that the split is uniformly better.
neurips-2022-on-analyzing-generative-and.tldr: An observed transition from generation to cleanup motivates splitting diffusion models into separate generator and denoiser components.

paragraphs: This paper studies how overparameterized three-layer neural tangent kernel models generalize after overfitting their training data. The analysis focuses on a specified collection of target functions called the learnable set. For those functions, the authors derive a test-error upper bound that decreases as either hidden layer gains more neurons.

Having two hidden layers introduces interactions absent from a two-layer model. The bound distinguishes their effects: it decreases faster with the width of the second hidden layer, nearer the output, than with the width of the first, nearer the input. This identifies an asymmetry in the theoretical bound, rather than guaranteeing that every observed test error must improve at those rates.

The authors also compare learnable sets and sensitivity to neuron biases. A three-layer NTK without bias has a learnable set no smaller than those of two-layer NTKs with various bias choices. Their results further suggest that actual three-layer generalization is much less sensitive to bias selection, especially at high input dimension. The conclusions concern this NTK setting and its specified target functions.
neurips-2022-on-the-generalization-power.tldr: For a specified learnable function set, three-layer NTK test-error bounds improve with width and favor expansion of the hidden layer nearer the output.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make predictions withstand input perturbations, but its benefits may differ across classes. This paper examines fairness as disparity in class-wise accuracy, particularly robust accuracy. It asks whether seeking stronger average robustness can make that disparity worse as the allowed perturbation radius increases.

The experiments find that larger perturbation radii in adversarial training produce greater differences in robust accuracy between classes. To investigate the effect theoretically, the authors analyze adversarially trained linear models under a Gaussian-mixture data distribution. That analysis supports the empirical observations and indicates that adversarial training can produce more serious robust-fairness problems than natural training.

Motivated by these theoretical findings, the authors propose fairly adversarial training, or FAT, to mitigate the tradeoff. Experiments validate the method's effectiveness. The work therefore connects a training choice to uneven class-level outcomes and uses the analysis to guide an intervention. Its fairness claim concerns differences among prediction classes, and the proposed method mitigates the reported tradeoff rather than establishing its complete elimination.
neurips-2022-on-the-tradeoff-between-rob.tldr: Stronger adversarial training can widen class-wise robustness disparities, and the proposed FAT method mitigates this empirically observed tradeoff.

paragraphs: WorldStrat addresses the difficulty of obtaining varied, high-resolution satellite imagery for machine learning. The dataset covers 10,000 square kilometers of unique locations, with Airbus SPOT imagery reaching 1.5 meters per pixel. Its sampling seeks broad representation of land uses, from agriculture and forests to ice caps and different urban densities.

The collection also includes locations often underrepresented in machine learning datasets, such as humanitarian sites, illegal mining areas, and settlements of people at risk. Each high-resolution image is temporally matched with multiple Sentinel-2 images at 10 meters per pixel. These paired observations support studying how several freely available lower-resolution images can contribute to a higher-resolution reconstruction.

The release includes efficient multi-frame super-resolution baselines and a Python package for rebuilding or extending the dataset, training models, and running inference. Matching the analytical value of costly imagery remains an aspiration, rather than an established outcome. Access terms also differ: high-resolution imagery has a noncommercial CC-BY-NC license, while labels, Sentinel-2 imagery, and weights use CC-BY, and code uses BSD.
neurips-2022-open-high-resolution-satell.tldr: WorldStrat pairs diverse high-resolution satellite imagery with repeated lower-resolution observations and provides tools and baselines for super-resolution research.

paragraphs: Radiance fields provide a compact three-dimensional representation that can synthesize images from new viewpoints. PeRFception explores using that representation directly for perception tasks. Instead of treating reconstructed scenes only as a way to render images, the paper makes radiance fields the input format for classification and segmentation.

Using Plenoxels, a variant of neural radiance fields, the authors construct large-scale datasets containing both object-centered and scene-centered scans. The format combines two-dimensional appearance and three-dimensional information in one representation. They report a 96.4% memory compression rate relative to the original dataset, demonstrating that this change in representation can substantially reduce storage requirements.

The authors build classification and segmentation models that consume the radiance fields directly. They also propose an augmentation technique intended to prevent models from overfitting to image backgrounds. The resulting contribution combines a data resource, a compact representation, and perception models built around that representation. It establishes a route for studying recognition and segmentation using reconstructed radiance fields, with the code and data made publicly available.
neurips-2022-perfception-perception-usin.tldr: PeRFception provides compact radiance-field datasets and models that use them directly for classification and segmentation.

paragraphs: Inverse rendering tries to infer properties of a scene from its images, but multiple explanations can fit the observations. This paper addresses that ambiguity by learning a prior over natural illumination. The focus is on representing plausible lighting, complementing approaches that emphasize prior knowledge about shape or surface appearance.

The proposed representation combines a variational auto-decoder with a SIREN neural field and extends Vector Neurons to build rotation equivariance into the network. This makes the model respond consistently to rotations. The resulting high dynamic range illumination model is compact while retaining the ability to represent complex, high-frequency structure in natural environment maps.

The authors train the model on a curated collection of 1,600 HDR environment maps of natural scenes and compare it with traditional representations. They demonstrate its use in an inverse-rendering task and in completing environment maps from partial observations. These applications show how a learned illumination prior can support both interpreting images and inferring missing lighting information, while explicitly respecting the rotational structure of the representation.
neurips-2022-rotation-equivariant-condit.tldr: A compact, rotation-equivariant neural illumination model learns natural lighting structure for inverse rendering and environment-map completion.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised semantic segmentation learns to label every pixel using a limited collection of annotated images plus unlabeled images. A central difficulty is that regions from the same class can look very different, even within one picture. That variation makes it hard to transfer label information reliably between individual pixels.

The paper addresses this through agreement between two predictors: a linear predictor and a prototype-based predictor. Encouraging consistent predictions implicitly pulls features assigned to the same pseudo-class toward at least one prototype of that class, while separating them from other classes' prototypes. Allowing proximity to one of several within-class prototypes accommodates appearance variation without requiring every instance of a class to share one feature pattern.

The full algorithm also incorporates CutMix and a strategy for maintaining the prototypes during training. Extensive evaluations on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes show superior performance over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support shaping the within-class feature distribution as a way to make label propagation more effective when dense annotations are scarce.
neurips-2022-semi-supervised-semantic-se.tldr: Agreement between linear and prototype-based predictors improves semi-supervised segmentation by organizing diverse features within each class.

paragraphs: TTOpt is an optimization procedure that combines an efficient quantized tensor train representation with a generalized maximum matrix volume principle. The paper brings these two mathematical ingredients together into a single optimizer. Its focus is on solving optimization tasks with favorable computational cost, assessed through function evaluations and execution time.

The authors demonstrate the method on tasks ranging from minimizing multidimensional functions to reinforcement learning. This range is significant because the proposed optimizer is presented as a procedure applicable across different optimization settings, rather than only as a solution for one particular objective. The tensor representation and matrix-volume principle form the common basis of those applications.

In the reported comparisons, TTOpt outperforms popular gradient-free methods in the number of function evaluations or execution time, often by a substantial margin. The distinction between those measures matters: the claim allows gains in either evaluation cost or elapsed computation, without asserting that both improve in every case. The stated findings support TTOpt as an efficient approach across the demonstrated tasks.
neurips-2022-ttopt-a-maximum-volume-quan.tldr: TTOpt combines quantized tensor trains and a matrix-volume principle to reduce evaluations or runtime against popular gradient-free optimizers.

paragraphs: Different vision tasks often motivate different model designs, requiring substantial task-specific expertise. UViM proposes a shared functional form for a range of tasks without such modifications. Its central idea is to divide prediction between a learned discrete guiding code and a model that produces the full visual output.

The system has two complementary components. An autoregressive language model learns to generate the guiding code, making use of its ability to model structured dependencies. A feed-forward base model learns to predict raw vision outputs while being guided by that code. This assigns structured coordination to the code-generating component and high-dimensional output production to the base model.

The authors evaluate the approach on panoptic segmentation, depth prediction, and image colorization. UViM achieves competitive, near state-of-the-art results across these three different tasks. Those findings support the proposed division of labor as a promising route toward unified vision modeling. They demonstrate breadth across the evaluated tasks while retaining the same overall model form, rather than establishing that one architecture has already solved every vision problem.
neurips-2022-uvim-a-unified-modeling-app.tldr: UViM combines autoregressively generated guiding codes with a feed-forward predictor to handle three diverse vision tasks using one model form.
